title: Caumsett
summary: Caumsett names Lloyd Neck in Huntington and connects the peninsula with stone, shoreline, Native place knowledge, and seventeenth-century land records. Caumsett names Lloyd Neck in Huntington, a peninsula bounded by Oyster Bay, Cow Harbor, and Long Island Sound. The existing polygon is a modern outline for the neck, not a surveyed colonial boundary.

why_this_matters: Caumsett preserves a Native name for Lloyd Neck, interpreted as a place near a sharp rock or whetstone-like stone. That meaning points to geology as part of Indigenous place knowledge: rocks were not just scenery, but useful materials connected to sharpening, work, and orientation. The North Shore appears here as a Native landscape where peninsulas, harbors, and stone resources were known and named with care.
history_content:
1687 Fort Neck/Lloyd Neck map

A 1687 hand-drawn map of Fort Neck / Lloyd Neck meadows preserves a colonial view of the same shoreline landscape now associated with Caumsett. The map is useful here because it shows how Native land use, meadow boundaries, colonial claims, and later Lloyd Neck disputes became layered onto one place.1
translation_content:
The name Caumsett is interpreted as at, about, or in the neighborhood of a sharp rock. The interpretation connects the name with Algonquian words for sharp and rock, including forms used for a whetstone or rock suitable for sharpening.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names can offer a way to reach further back to the past, to act as ruins of culture.”

— Ashna Abdulrahman Kareem Zada, The Geographical Names of Provinces in Iraq (2018), Abstract

Place-name history should show Native people as active and present, not only as names in old documents.
land_loss_content: The 1654 deed is the key dated record for this placename. Full deed wording and page details are kept in the reference system so the public text can stay concise and reviewable.
whereintheworld_content: Caumsett links a still-visible Huntington landscape with a Native placename and a documented seventeenth-century land transaction. The name also preserves attention to stone, shoreline, and use of place rather than only colonial ownership boundaries.
